Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

citations.quote: Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. Two nonzero vectors $x,y\in H$ represent the same **ray** when $y=\alpha x$ for some nonzero $\alpha\in\mathbb C$. A **pure state** is such a ray. If $u$ is a unit representative, its associated operator is $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$, with the bra, ket and outer-product convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]. The theorem [[thm-qc-ray-projector-well-defined-and-bijective]] proves that this operator is a rank-one orthogonal projection independent of the chosen unit representative, so it is the operator representative of the pure state.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex-inner-product spaces with the tensor-product convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For every $\Psi\in H\otimes K$ there are an integer $r\ge0$, positive numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_r$, and orthonormal families $u_1,\ldots,u_r\in H$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_r\in K$ such that

$$\Psi=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j u_j\otimes v_j,\qquad \|\Psi\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j^2.$$

For $\Psi=0$ take $r=0$ and the empty sum. For any chosen ordered pair of orthonormal bases, the construction below obtains the $s_j$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient matrix of $\Psi$ in their ordered product basis.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$. Its **row space** $\operatorname{Row}(A)\subseteq F^n$ is the span of its rows, its **column space** $\operatorname{Col}(A)\subseteq F^m$ is the span of its columns, and its **nullspace** is
$$N(A):=\{x\in F^n:Ax=0\}.$$

The **row rank** and **column rank** are
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Row}(A),\qquad \operatorname{crank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Col}(A).$$
These dimensions are defined because each space is spanned by a finite list.
Starting with the empty list, inspect the spanning vectors in order and retain a
vector exactly when it is not in the span of those already retained. Induction
shows that the retained list is independent and has the same span as the
original finite list, so it is a finite basis. The **rank** of $A$ is its row
rank; [[thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank]] proves that it also equals the column
rank.

For every finite matrix over a field,
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A)=\operatorname{crank}(A).$$
Both dimensions equal the number of pivots in any echelon form of $A$.
For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the matrix rank of $A$ equals the rank of the linear map $L_A:F^n\to F^m$ defined by $L_A(x)=Ax$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. Then $\operatorname{rank} T$ equals the number of positive
singular values of $T$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: Choose ordered orthonormal bases of $H_A,H_B$ using [F5], and let $C$ be the coefficient matrix of $\psi$ in their product basis [L2]. For any other ordered orthonormal bases, let $A,B$ have the new basis vectors as columns in the old coordinates. Their columns are orthonormal, so the finite row-by-column identities $A^*A=B^*B=I$ hold; because they are basis changes, both matrices are invertible and hence unitary. Expanding the new product basis vectors in the old one and using conjugate-linearity in the second argument gives $c'_{pq}=\sum_{i,k}\overline{A_{ip}}c_{ik}\overline{B_{kq}}$, so the new coefficient matrix is $C'=A^*C\overline B$. The factors $A^*$ and $\overline B$ are invertible, so the map represented by $C'=A^*C\overline B$ is $A^*\circ T_C\circ\overline B$, where $T_C$ is the map represented by $C$. Since $\overline B$ is onto, its image is $A^*(\operatorname{im}T_C)$; since $A^*$ is injective, this image has the same dimension as $\operatorname{im}T_C$. By [F2], the matrix rank is therefore unchanged, so it is basis-independent. Multiplying $\psi$ by any nonzero scalar multiplies $C$ by that scalar and also preserves its rank.

In any Schmidt decomposition $\psi=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j u_j\otimes v_j$ with all $s_j>0$ and orthonormal factor families, tensor coordinates multiply, so its coefficient matrix is $C=U D V^{\mathsf T}$, where the columns of $U,V$ are the coordinates of the $u_j,v_j$ and $D=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_r)$. The orthonormal columns give $U^*U=V^*V=I_r$, so $U$ is injective; conjugating $V^*V=I_r$ gives $V^{\mathsf T}\overline V=I_r$, so $V^{\mathsf T}$ is surjective; and $D$ is invertible. Thus $\operatorname{rank}(C)=r$. Conversely, [L3] constructs such a Schmidt decomposition from the SVD, and [F3] and [F4] show that its number of positive coefficients is the rank of $C$. Therefore the number of terms is the same for every Schmidt decomposition and equals the defined Schmidt rank.

If $\psi=c(a\otimes b)$ for nonzero $a,b,c$, its coefficient matrix is $c\alpha\beta^{\mathsf T}$ for the coordinate columns $\alpha,\beta$, so its rank is one. Conversely, if $C$ has rank one, choose a nonzero column $\alpha$; every column is a scalar multiple $\beta_k\alpha$, so $C=\alpha\beta^{\mathsf T}$ with $\beta\ne0$. The coefficient expansion then gives $\psi=a\otimes b$ for the vectors with coordinates $\alpha,\beta$. Thus the ray is a product ray exactly when the Schmidt rank is one.

Since $\psi\ne0$, its coefficient matrix is nonzero and has positive rank. By the product-ray equivalence in step 2.1, failure to be a product ray is equivalent to Schmidt rank greater than one, which is precisely entanglement by the Definition.

By [L4], the common operator is a density operator, so the outcome law [L2] defines its weight for each effect $E_a$. Since the density operator is identical for $u$ and $\lambda u$, those weights agree; [L5] proves the finite family of weights is a probability distribution.

Since $x=\|x\|u$ with $\|x\|$ a nonnegative real, [F1] and [L3] give $|x\rangle\langle x|=\|x\|^2|u\rangle\langle u|$. **The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

An endomorphism $P$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space is the orthogonal projection onto some subspace if and only if

$$P^2=P\qquad\text{and}\qquad P^*=P.$$

In that case it is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{im}P$, along $\ker P=(\operatorname{im}P)^\perp$. The cases $P=0$ and $P=I$ are included.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, the following are equivalent:

1. $T$ preserves norms.
2. $T$ preserves inner products.
3. $T$ sends every orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
4. $T$ sends some orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
5. $T^*T=I$.

Whenever these conditions hold, $T$ is invertible and $T^{-1}=T^*$, so also $TT^*=I$. The zero-dimensional case is included.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: By [L1], $\Pi_\psi x=\langle x,\psi\rangle_{\rm root}\psi$. Then $\Pi_\psi^2x=\langle x,\psi\rangle\langle\psi,\psi\rangle\psi=\Pi_\psi x$. Also $\langle\Pi_\psi x,y\rangle=\langle x,\psi\rangle\langle\psi,y\rangle=\langle x,\Pi_\psi y\rangle$ by [F1] and [F2]; uniqueness [F3] gives $\Pi_\psi^*=\Pi_\psi$. Its image is contained in $\mathbb C\psi$ and $\Pi_\psi\psi=\psi$, hence its range is exactly one-dimensional.

The self-adjoint idempotent result [F4] makes $\Pi_\psi$ an orthogonal projection. For $|\lambda|=1$, [L1] and [F1] give $\Pi_{\lambda\psi}x=\langle x,\lambda\psi\rangle\lambda\psi=\overline\lambda\lambda\langle x,\psi\rangle\psi=\Pi_\psi x$ for every $x$.

If $v$ is any other unit representative of the ray of $\psi$, [L2] gives $v=c\psi$ for some nonzero scalar $c$. By [F1] and [F5], $1=\|v\|^2=\langle c\psi,c\psi\rangle=|c|^2\langle\psi,\psi\rangle=|c|^2$, so $|c|=1$. Step 2.1 then gives $\Pi_v=\Pi_\psi$, and both reflection signs depend only on the ray.

Applying [L4] to $\Pi_\psi$ gives both standalone reflections as unitary involutions and $C(S_\psi)=(Z_C)C(R_\psi)$. Since $S_\psi=-R_\psi$, their standalone outputs differ only by the scalar $-1$ and represent the same ray.

Choose an ordered orthonormal basis of $H$ using [F7]. Together with the control basis from [L6], it supplies the factor bases required by [L7], whose proof shows the pairing is independent of this choice. Because $\psi\in\operatorname{ran}\Pi_\psi$, [L4] gives $R_\psi\psi=\psi$ and $S_\psi\psi=-\psi$. The controlled input $|+\rangle\otimes\psi$ therefore becomes $|+\rangle\otimes\psi$ under $C(R_\psi)$ and $| -\rangle\otimes\psi$ under $C(S_\psi)$. Since $|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, [L6] gives $\langle+,-\rangle=\frac12(\langle0,0\rangle-\langle0,1\rangle+\langle1,0\rangle-\langle1,1\rangle)=0$ and $\langle+,+\rangle=\langle-,-\rangle=1$. By [L7], the two joint outputs are unit and orthogonal. Orthogonal nonzero vectors are not nonzero scalar multiples, so the ray definition [L2] makes the output rays distinct and the control sign relative.

Let $U$ be unitary and let $\psi=Ua$ for the specified unit input $a\in H$. For any $z\in H$, [L1] gives $U|a\rangle\langle a|U^\dagger z=U\bigl(\langle U^\dagger z,a\rangle_{\rm root}a\bigr)=\langle U^\dagger z,a\rangle_{\rm root}\psi$. The adjoint identity [F2] with $v=a,w=z$, followed by conjugate symmetry [F1], gives $\langle U^\dagger z,a\rangle_{\rm root}=\langle z,Ua\rangle_{\rm root}=\langle z,\psi\rangle_{\rm root}$. Thus $U|a\rangle\langle a|U^\dagger=\Pi_\psi$ as operators. By [F6], $UU^\dagger=U^\dagger U=I$, so conjugating $R_a=2|a\rangle\langle a|-I$ and $S_a=I-2|a\rangle\langle a|$ gives $R_\psi$ and $S_\psi$, respectively. The algebraic equality does not grant the calls: [L5] requires inverse availability and its cost to be stated separately.

citations.quote: Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and $U:H\to H$ a unitary. Let $\theta\in\mathbb R$, and suppose the model separately grants controlled access to both $U$ and $e^{i\theta}U$. There is a normalized eigenvector $\phi$ with $U\phi=\mu\phi$ and $|\mu|=1$. Let $C=Q_2=\mathbb C^2$ be the control qubit with ordered computational basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$; define $|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and prepare $(|0\rangle+\overline\mu|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ with target $\phi$. The two joint effects are $E_\pm=|\pm\rangle\langle\pm|\otimes I_H$. The $E_+$ outcome has probability $1$ after $C(U)$ and $\cos^2(\theta/2)$ after $C(e^{i\theta}U)$. Thus the two controlled maps give different outcome laws exactly when $\theta\notin2\pi\mathbb Z$; when $\theta\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, the controlled maps coincide. This is a mathematical witness; it does not assert that controlled access or the witness-state preparation is free.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with the root pairing linear in its first argument, and let $u\in H$ satisfy $\|u\|=1$. Define $P_u:=|u\rangle\langle u|$ by the root-linear-first Dirac convention. Then $P_u$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, has one-dimensional range, is non-negative, and has trace one. In particular, $P_u$ is a density operator.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

Let $\rho$ be a density operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$, and let $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite POVM on $H$. Then

$$p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)\in[0,1]\quad\text{for each }a\in\Omega,\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}p_\rho(a)=1.$$

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

derivations.claim: In the ordered basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$, the first controlled block is $C(I_2)=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&I_2\end{pmatrix}=I_4$. It sends the input to $\omega_0=|+\rangle\otimes|0\rangle$. Both factors are unit vectors by [L7], so their product is unit by [L6], and its rank-one projector is a density operator by [L4]. In [L1], specialize $U=I_2$, $\phi=|0\rangle$, and $\mu=1$; its verified control POVM then gives plus probability $1$.

The separately granted second block is $C(e^{i\theta}I_2)=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&e^{i\theta}I_2\end{pmatrix}=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,e^{i\theta},e^{i\theta})$. It sends the input to $\omega_\theta=\chi_\theta\otimes|0\rangle$, where $\chi_\theta=(|0\rangle+e^{i\theta}|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. By [L3] and [L7], $\langle+|\chi_\theta\rangle_D=\langle\chi_\theta,+\rangle_{\rm root}=(1+e^{i\theta})/2$. The phase identity [F1] and orthonormality [L7] give $\|\chi_\theta\|^2=(1+|e^{i\theta}|^2)/2=1$; then the product pairing [L6] gives $\|\omega_\theta\|=1$. Its projector is a density operator by [L4], so the outcome law [L5] applies and gives $|(1+e^{i\theta})/2|^2$, which equals $\cos^2(\theta/2)$ by the derivation in the proof of [L1].

At $\theta=0$, the second controlled matrix is $I_4$ and its plus probability is $1$. At $\theta=\pi$, its diagonal is $(1,1,-1,-1)$ and its plus probability is $0$. The minus probability is the complement by normalization [L8], so these are distinct finite outcome laws under the explicit separate-access assumption.
